column2: And she, to wide-spaced Lacedaemon, Pallas Athena
went, to the glorious son of great-hearted Odysseus,
to remind him of his return and to urge him to go home.
And she found Telemachus and the splendid son of Nestor
sleeping in the forecourt of glorious Menelaus,
the son of Nestor indeed overcome by soft sleep;
but Telemachus sweet sleep did not hold, but in his heart
through the ambrosial night cares for his father kept him awake.
And standing near grey-eyed Athena spoke:

Telemachus, it is no longer good to wander far from home,
11	leaving your possessions and men in your house
12	so overbearing; lest they eat up all
13	your possessions, dividing them, and you make a fruitless journey.
14	But urge Menelaus, good at the war-cry, at once
15	to send you off, that you may still find your blameless mother at home.
16	For already her father and her brothers bid her
17	marry Eurymachus; for he surpasses all
18	the suitors in gifts and has increased the bridal gifts;
19	lest some possession be carried from your house against your will.
20	For you know what kind of spirit is in a woman's breast;
21	she wishes to enrich the house of the man who marries her,
22	and of her former children and her dear wedded husband
23	she no longer remembers when he is dead, nor asks about him.
24	But you, going yourself, entrust everything
25	to whichever of the maidservants seems to you the best,
26	until the gods show you a glorious wife.
27	And another word I shall tell you, and you lay it up in your heart.
28	The chief of the suitors lie in wait for you on purpose
29	in the strait between Ithaca and rugged Samos,
30	eager to kill you before you reach your fatherland.
31	But I think not; before that the earth will hold some
32	of the suitors, who devour your livelihood.
33	But keep your well-built ship far from the islands,
34	and sail by night as well; and a wind will be sent you from behind
35	by whichever of the immortals guards and protects you.
36	And when you reach the first shore of Ithaca,
37	send the ship to the city with all your comrades,
38	and you yourself go first of all to the swineherd,
39	who is the keeper of your pigs, and is likewise kindly to you.
40	Spend the night there; and send him to the city
41	to tell the news to prudent Penelope
42	that you are safe and have come from Pylos.
So saying she went away to high Olympus,
and he roused the son of Nestor from sweet sleep
nudging him with his foot, and spoke to him:

Wake, Pisistratus son of Nestor, bring the whole-hoofed horses
47	and yoke them under the chariot, that we may accomplish the journey.
And Pisistratus son of Nestor answered him:

Telemachus, there is no way, however eager for the journey,
50	to drive through the dark night; and soon it will be dawn.
51	But wait until the hero son of Atreus, Menelaus famed for his spear,
52	brings gifts and puts them on the chariot,
53	and sends us off, speaking to us with gentle words.
54	For a guest remembers all his days
55	the host who has shown him friendship.
So he spoke, and at once golden-throned Dawn came.
And close to them came Menelaus, good at the war-cry,
having risen from his bed beside fair-haired Helen.
And when the dear son of Odysseus noticed him,
hastening, he put a shining tunic about his skin,
and the hero threw a great cloak over his stout shoulders,
and went out of doors, and standing by him spoke
Telemachus, the dear son of divine Odysseus:
And then Menelaus, good at the war-cry, answered him:

Telemachus, I shall not keep you here a long time
69	when you are eager to return; and I disapprove of another
70	host who loves a guest exceedingly,
71	or hates him exceedingly; better is everything in measure.
72	It is an equal evil, to urge a guest to go
73	when he is unwilling, and to hold back one who hurries.
74	One must befriend a guest who is present, and send him off if he wishes.
75	But wait until I bring fair gifts and put them on the chariot,
76	and you see them with your eyes, and I tell the women
77	to prepare a meal in the hall of what is within.
78	Both glory and splendour and benefit it is
79	to go on one's way over the boundless earth having dined.
80	And if you wish to turn through Hellas and the middle of Argos,
81	so that I may follow you myself, and yoke horses for you,
82	and lead you to the cities of men; and none will
83	send us away empty, but will give us one thing at least to carry,
84	either a bronze tripod or a cauldron,
85	or two mules or a golden cup.
And discreet Telemachus answered him:

Menelaus son of Atreus, Zeus-nurtured, leader of the people,
88	I wish to go home now; for when I left I did not leave
89	anyone behind to watch over my possessions;
90	lest while seeking my godlike father I perish myself,
91	or some fine treasure be lost from my halls.
And when Menelaus, good at the war-cry, heard this,
at once he bade his wife and the maidservants
to prepare a meal in the hall of what was within.
And close to him came Eteoneus son of Boethous,
having risen from his bed, for he did not live far from him;
Menelaus, good at the war-cry, bade him kindle a fire
and roast some meat; and he did not disobey on hearing.
And he himself went down into the fragrant chamber,
not alone; with him went Helen and Megapenthes.
But when they came where the treasures lay,
then the son of Atreus took a two-handled cup,
and bade his son Megapenthes carry a silver
mixing-bowl; and Helen stood by the chests,
where were the richly embroidered robes, which she herself had made.
Helen, bright among women, lifted one of these and carried it,
which was the most beautiful in its embroideries and the largest,
and shone like a star; and it lay lowest of the others.
And they went on through the house, until they came to
Telemachus; and fair-haired Menelaus spoke to him:

Telemachus, as for your return, as you purpose in your heart,
112	so may Zeus accomplish it, loud-thundering husband of Hera.
113	And of the gifts, as many treasures as lie in my house,
114	I shall give what is the most beautiful and most precious.
115	I shall give you a wrought mixing-bowl; it is all
116	of silver, and its rims are finished with gold,
117	the work of Hephaestus; the hero Phaedimus gave it to me,
118	king of the Sidonians, when his house sheltered me
119	there on my return; to you I wish to give it.
So saying, the hero son of Atreus put the two-handled cup
in his hand; and strong Megapenthes
brought the shining bowl, of silver, and set it before him;
and fair-cheeked Helen stood by
holding a robe in her hands, and spoke a word and addressed him:

I too give you this gift, dear child,
126	a memorial of Helen's hands, for the time of your much-desired marriage,
127	for your wife to wear; but till then let it lie
128	in the hall with your dear mother. And may you come
129	gladly to your well-built house and your fatherland.
So saying she put it in his hands, and he received it gladly.
And these things the hero Pisistratus put in the chest,
receiving them, and marvelled at it all in his heart.
And fair-haired Menelaus led them to the house.
And they sat down on couches and chairs.
A handmaid poured water for the hands from a jug, bringing it
in a fair golden one, over a silver basin,
to wash; and she drew up a polished table beside.
And the revered housekeeper brought bread and set it by,
adding many dishes, giving freely of what was there.
And beside them the son of Boethous carved the meat and distributed shares;
and the son of glorious Menelaus poured the wine.
And they put out their hands to the food ready laid before them.
But when they had put away desire for drink and food,
then Telemachus and the splendid son of Nestor
yoked the horses and mounted the richly decorated chariot,
and drove out of the forecourt and the echoing portico.
And after them went the son of Atreus, fair-haired Menelaus,
holding honey-sweet wine in his right hand,
in a golden cup, so that they might pour a libation before going.
He stood before the horses, and pledging them spoke:

Farewell, young men, and tell Nestor, shepherd of the people,
152	for to me he was as kindly as a father,
153	while we sons of the Achaeans fought in Troy.
And discreet Telemachus answered him:

Indeed, Zeus-nurtured, as you say,
156	we shall tell him all this when we come; would that I
157	might return to Ithaca and, finding Odysseus in the house,
158	say that having met with all kindness from you
159	I come, and bring many fine treasures.
As he spoke thus, a bird flew on the right,
an eagle carrying in its talons a huge white goose,
a tame one from the yard; and shouting they followed,
men and women; and it, coming near them,
darted on the right before the horses; and they, seeing it,
rejoiced, and the heart in all their breasts was warmed.
And among them Pisistratus son of Nestor began to speak:

Consider, Menelaus Zeus-nurtured, leader of the people,
168	whether a god showed this portent to us two or to yourself.
So he spoke, and Menelaus dear to Ares pondered
how, understanding it, he might interpret it fittingly.
And long-robed Helen, anticipating him, spoke a word:

Hear me; and I shall prophesy, as the immortals cast it in my heart
173	and as I think it will be fulfilled.
174	As this bird snatched the goose, reared in the house,
175	coming from the mountain, where is its kin and brood,
176	so Odysseus, having suffered many evils and wandered much,
177	will come home and take vengeance; or even now
178	he is at home, and devises evil for all the suitors.
And discreet Telemachus answered her:

So now may Zeus grant it, loud-thundering husband of Hera;
181	then even there I would pray to you as to a god.
He spoke, and laid the whip on the horses; and they very quickly
darted to the plain through the city, eager.
And all day long they shook the yoke, holding it on both sides.
And the sun set and all the ways were shadowed;
and they came to Pherae, to the house of Diocles,
son of Ortilochus, whom Alpheius begot as a child.
There they spent the night; and he set hospitality beside them.
And when early-born rosy-fingered Dawn appeared,
they yoked the horses and mounted the richly decorated chariot,
and drove out of the forecourt and the echoing portico;
he whipped them on to drive, and they flew not unwilling.
And soon they came to the steep citadel of Pylos;
and then Telemachus spoke to the son of Nestor:

Son of Nestor, how could you promise and fulfil
196	a word of mine? We claim to be guest-friends continually
197	from the friendship of our fathers, and we are also of an age;
198	and this journey will bring us still more to one mind.
199	Do not take me past my ship, Zeus-nurtured, but leave me here,
200	lest the old man hold me against my will in his house,
201	eager to entertain me; and I must get home more quickly.
So he spoke, and the son of Nestor thought in his own heart
how he might promise and fulfil it fittingly for him.
And as he thought, this seemed to him the better course:
he turned the horses to the swift ship and the sea-shore,
and set the fair gifts in the stern of the ship,
the clothing and gold, which Menelaus had given him;
and urging him he spoke winged words:

Quickly now embark and call all your comrades,
210	before I reach home and tell the old man.
211	For I know this well in my mind and in my heart:
212	such is the old man's overbearing spirit, he will not let you go,
213	but will himself come here to call you, and I do not think
214	he will go back empty; for he will be exceedingly angry in any case.
So speaking he drove the fair-maned horses
back to the city of the Pylians, and quickly reached the house.
And Telemachus urged on his comrades and ordered:

Put the gear in order, comrades, in the black ship,
219	and let us embark ourselves, that we may accomplish our journey.
So he spoke, and they listened to him and obeyed,
and quickly went aboard and sat at the oars.
He indeed was busy at this and praying, and sacrificing to Athena
by the stern of the ship; and near him came a man
from far away, fleeing from Argos, having killed a man,
a seer; and in lineage he was a descendant of Melampus,
who once dwelt in Pylos, mother of flocks,
rich among the Pylians, dwelling in a house exceeding great;
then he came to the land of others, fleeing his fatherland
and great-hearted Neleus, most glorious of the living,
who for a full year held much of his wealth
by force. And he meanwhile in the halls of Phylacus
was bound in grievous bonds, suffering strong pains
for the sake of Neleus's daughter and a heavy delusion,
which the dread goddess Erinys had put in his mind.
But he escaped his doom and drove the lowing cattle
to Pylos from Phylace and avenged the shameful deed
on godlike Neleus, and brought the woman
to the house of his brother. And he came to the land of others,
to horse-nurturing Argos; for there it was fated for him
to dwell, ruling over many Argives.
There he married a wife and built a high-roofed house,
and begot Antiphates and Mantius, two strong sons.
Antiphates begot great-hearted Oicles,
and Oicles Amphiaraus, rouser of the people,
whom aegis-bearing Zeus and Apollo loved at heart
with every kind of love; yet he did not reach the threshold of old age,
but perished in Thebes because of a woman's gifts.
His sons were Alcmaeon and Amphilochus.
Mantius in turn begot Polypheides and Cleitus;
but golden-throned Dawn snatched Cleitus
for his beauty, that he might be among the immortals;
and high-spirited Polypheides the seer Apollo
made by far the best of mortals, after Amphiaraus died;
who removed to Hyperesia, angry with his father,
and dwelling there he prophesied to all mortals.
His son came up, and Theoclymenus was his name,
who now stood near Telemachus; and he found him
pouring libations and praying by the swift black ship,
and he spoke to him winged words:

Friend, since I find you sacrificing in this place,
261	I beseech you by your sacrifices and the god, and then
262	by your own head and the comrades who follow you,
263	tell me, who ask, the truth, and do not hide it:
264	who are you among men, and from where? Where is your city and parents?
And discreet Telemachus answered him:

Well then, stranger, I shall tell you very exactly.
267	I am by race from Ithaca, and my father is Odysseus,
268	if ever he was; but now he has perished by a grievous death.
269	For this reason I have taken comrades and a black ship
270	and come to inquire about my father long gone.
And godlike Theoclymenus said to him in turn:

So I too am from my fatherland, having killed a man
273	of my tribe; and many are the brothers and kinsmen
274	in horse-nurturing Argos, and they rule greatly over the Achaeans.
275	Avoiding them, death and black doom,
276	I flee, since it is my fate to wander among men.
277	But set me on your ship, since fleeing I have begged you,
278	lest they kill me; for I think they are pursuing.
And discreet Telemachus answered him:

I shall not indeed drive you away from the balanced ship if you wish,
281	but follow; and there you will be befriended with what we have.
So speaking he took from him his bronze spear,
and laid it along the deck of the curved ship;
and he himself went aboard the sea-going ship.
In the stern then he sat down, and beside himself
he seated Theoclymenus; and they loosed the stern cables.
And Telemachus urged on his comrades and ordered them
to lay hold of the tackle; and they hastily obeyed.
They raised the fir mast and set it in the hollow
mast-box, and bound it with forestays,
and hauled up the white sails with well-twisted ox-hide ropes.
And grey-eyed Athena sent them a fair wind,
blowing strongly through the upper air, that as quickly as possible
the ship might run through the salt water of the sea.
They went past Cruni and fair-flowing Chalcis.
And the sun set and all the ways were shadowed;
and she approached Pheae, urged on by the wind of Zeus,
and past divine Elis, where the Epeians rule.
From there again she steered towards the Pointed Islands,
pondering whether he would escape death or be caught.
And those two in the hut, Odysseus and the divine swineherd,
were having supper; and with them the other men were having supper.
But when they had put away desire for drink and food,
Odysseus spoke among them, testing the swineherd,
whether he would still treat him kindly and bid him stay
there at the farmstead, or urge him to the city:

Hear me now, Eumaeus, and all you other comrades:
308	in the morning I long to go away to the city
309	to beg, so that I may not wear you out and your comrades.
310	But advise me well and give me a good guide with me
311	who will lead me there; and in the city I shall myself, by necessity,
312	wander, in case someone gives me a cup and a loaf.
313	And going to the house of divine Odysseus
314	I might give news to prudent Penelope,
315	and I might mingle with the overbearing suitors,
316	if they would give me a meal, having countless good things.
317	Quickly I could serve well among them in whatever they wished.
318	For I shall tell you, and you attend and listen to me:
319	by the favour of Hermes the guide, who gives grace and glory
320	to the works of all men,
321	in service no other mortal could vie with me,
322	in laying a fire well and splitting dry wood,
323	in carving and roasting and pouring wine,
324	such as inferiors do for their betters.
And greatly vexed you said to him, swineherd Eumaeus:

Alas, stranger, why has this thought come into your mind?
327	Surely you long to perish there altogether,
328	if you wish to go down into the throng of the suitors,
329	whose violence and force reach the iron heaven.
330	Their servants are not like you,
331	but young men, well clothed in cloaks and tunics,
332	always sleek in their heads and fair faces,
333	who serve them; and the polished tables
334	are laden with bread and meat and wine.
335	But stay; for no one is vexed by you being here,
336	neither I nor any other of the comrades I have.
337	And when the dear son of Odysseus comes,
338	he will clothe you in a cloak and tunic as garments,
339	and send you where your heart and spirit bid.
And much-enduring divine Odysseus answered him:

Would that you, Eumaeus, may be as dear to father Zeus
342	as to me, since you have stopped my wandering and dread misery.
343	There is nothing worse for mortals than roaming;
344	but because of the accursed belly men have evil cares,
345	whomever wandering and woe and pain come upon.
346	Now since you hold me back and bid me wait for him,
347	come, tell me about the mother of divine Odysseus
348	and his father, whom he left on the threshold of old age when he went,
349	whether they are still alive beneath the rays of the sun,
350	or are already dead and in the house of Hades.
And again the swineherd, leader of men, said to him:

Well then, stranger, I shall tell you very exactly.
353	Laertes is still alive, but prays to Zeus always
354	that his spirit may waste away from his limbs in his house;
355	for he grieves terribly for his son who is gone
356	and for his wedded wife, wise in mind, who most of all
357	grieved him by dying and put him in raw old age.
358	She died of grief for her glorious son,
359	by a wretched death, may no one die so who is
360	dear to me here and does me kindness.
361	As long as she was alive, though grieving, nevertheless
362	so long it was dear to me to ask and inquire,
363	because she herself reared me together with long-robed Ctimene,
364	her mighty daughter, whom she bore youngest of her children;
365	with her I was reared, and she honoured me only a little less.
366	But when we both reached lovely youth,
367	her they gave away to Same and took countless gifts,
368	but me she clothed in a cloak and tunic, as garments,
369	very fair, and gave me sandals for my feet,
370	and sent me to the country; and she loved me more in her heart.
371	Now I lack these things; but for me the blessed gods
372	prosper the work at which I abide;
373	from this I have eaten and drunk and given to the respected.
374	But from my mistress it is not pleasant to hear
375	either word or deed, since evil has fallen on the house,
376	overbearing men; and servants greatly desire
377	to speak face to face with their mistress and ask about each thing,
378	and to eat and drink, and then to carry something
379	to the country, such as always warms the heart of servants.
And answering him wise Odysseus said:

Alas, how you, Eumaeus swineherd, while still small,
382	were driven far from your fatherland and parents.
383	But come, tell me this and recount it truly,
384	whether the broad-wayed city of men was sacked,
385	in which your father and lady mother dwelt,
386	or whether, left alone by the sheep or the cattle,
387	hostile men took you in ships and sold you
388	to this man's house, and he gave a worthy price.
And again the swineherd, leader of men, said to him:

Stranger, since you ask me and inquire about this,
391	now listen in silence and enjoy yourself, and drink wine
392	sitting. These nights are immeasurable; there is time to sleep,
393	and there is time to listen with pleasure; and you need not
394	lie down before the hour; much sleep too is a grief.
395	Of the others, whomever heart and spirit bid,
396	let him go out and sleep; and when dawn appears
397	let him eat and follow the master's swine.
398	But we two in the hut, drinking and feasting,
399	let us take pleasure in each other's grievous troubles,
400	remembering; for a man takes pleasure even in pains afterwards,
401	whoever has suffered very much and wandered much.
402	And this I shall tell you which you ask and inquire.
403	There is an island called Syria, if you have perhaps heard,
404	above Ortygia, where are the turnings of the sun,
405	not very populous, but good,
406	good for cattle, good for sheep, rich in wine, abounding in grain.
407	Hunger never enters the people, nor any other
408	hateful sickness falls upon wretched mortals;
409	but when the tribes of men grow old in the city,
410	silver-bowed Apollo comes with Artemis
411	and with his gentle shafts attacks and slays them.
412	There are two cities, and everything is divided between them;
413	and over both of them my father was king,
414	Ctesius son of Ormenus, like the immortals.
415	There came Phoenician men, famed for ships,
416	traders, bringing countless trinkets in a black ship.
417	In my father's house was a Phoenician woman,
418	fair and tall and skilled in splendid works;
419	her the crafty Phoenicians deceived.
420	First one lay with her as she washed beside the hollow ship
421	in bed and love, which deceives the minds
422	of women, even of one who is virtuous.
423	Then he asked who she was and where she came from;
424	and she at once pointed out her father's high-roofed house:
425	'I claim to be from Sidon rich in bronze,
426	and I am the daughter of Arybas, flowing with wealth;
427	but Taphian pirates snatched me
428	as I was coming from the field, and brought me here and sold me
429	to this man's house; and he gave a worthy price.'
430	And the man who lay with her in secret said to her:
431	'Would you now go back again with us to your home,
432	to see the high-roofed house of your father and mother
433	and themselves? For they are still living and are called rich.'
434	And the woman answered him and said:
435	'This could be, if you sailors would be willing
436	to pledge me with an oath that you will bring me home unharmed.'
437	So she spoke, and they all swore as she bade.
438	But when they had sworn and completed the oath,
439	again the woman spoke among them and answered:
440	'Silence now, let none of your comrades speak to me
441	with words, meeting me in the street,
442	or perhaps at the spring; lest someone go to the old man
443	at the house and tell, and he suspect and bind me
444	in grievous bonds, and devise destruction for you.
445	But keep the word in your minds, and hasten the purchase of provisions.
446	And when the ship is full of goods,
447	let a message come quickly to me at the house;
448	for I shall bring gold too, whatever comes to my hand;
449	and I would willingly give something else as passage-money.
450	For I nurse in the hall the child of my master,
451	a clever one, already running out of doors with me;
452	him I would bring on the ship, and he would fetch you countless price,
453	wherever you sell him among men of foreign speech.'
454	So saying she went away to the fair house,
455	and they for a whole year staying with us there
456	traded for much livelihood in the hollow ship.
457	But when the hollow ship was loaded for going,
458	then they sent a messenger to tell the woman.
459	A man very cunning came to my father's house
460	with a golden necklace, strung with amber.
461	This in the hall the maidservants and my lady mother
462	handled with their hands and looked at with their eyes,
463	promising a price; and he nodded to her in silence.
464	Then he, having nodded, went to the hollow ship,
465	and she, taking me by the hand, led me out of the house.
466	And in the forecourt she found cups and tables
467	of the feasting men, who were attending on my father.
468	They had gone out to the place of council and the talk of the people,
469	and she quickly hid three cups in her bosom
470	and carried them out; and I followed in my folly.
471	And the sun set, and all the ways were shadowed;
472	and we went quickly to the famous harbour,
473	where was the swift ship of the Phoenician men.
474	They then went aboard and sailed the watery paths,
475	taking us two aboard; and Zeus sent a wind.
476	For six days we sailed alike by night and day;
477	but when Zeus son of Kronos brought the seventh day,
478	then Artemis the archer struck the woman,
479	and she thudded into the bilge like a sea-gull.
480	And her they threw out to be prey for seals and fishes;
481	but I was left behind, grieved at heart.
482	And the wind and water brought them to Ithaca,
483	where Laertes bought me with his possessions.
484	Thus I saw this land with my eyes.
And Zeus-born Odysseus answered him with a word:

Eumaeus, you have greatly stirred the spirit in my breast
487	telling each of these things, all the pains you suffered in your heart.
488	But indeed Zeus has set good beside the evil for you,
489	since after much toil you came to the house of a kindly
490	man, who provides you with food and drink
491	with care, and you live a good life; but I
492	come here wandering through many cities of mortals.
So they spoke such things to one another,
and slept not long, but a little;
for soon fair-throned Dawn came. And on the shore
Telemachus's comrades loosed the sails and took down the mast
quickly, and rowed the ship into the mooring with oars;
they threw out the anchor-stones, and tied the stern cables;
and they themselves too went out onto the breaking edge of the sea,
and prepared a meal and mixed gleaming wine.
But when they had put away desire for drink and food,
discreet Telemachus began to speak among them:

You now drive the black ship to the city,
504	but I shall go to the fields and the herdsmen;
505	and in the evening, having seen my farms, I shall go down to the city.
506	And in the morning I shall set out for you a wayfarer's meal,
507	a good feast of meat and sweet-drinking wine.
And godlike Theoclymenus said to him in turn:

And where, dear child, am I to go? To whose house shall I come
510	of the men who rule over rugged Ithaca?
511	Or shall I go straight to your mother and your house?
And discreet Telemachus answered him:

In other circumstances I would bid you also
514	come to our house; for there is no lack of hospitality; but for you yourself
515	it would be worse, since I shall be away, and your mother
516	will not see you; for she does not often appear
517	among the suitors in the house, but weaves a web upstairs, away from them.
518	But I point you to another man whom you may visit,
519	Eurymachus, the splendid son of wise Polybus,
520	whom the Ithacans now look upon equal to a god;
521	for he is by far the best man and most eager
522	to marry my mother and to have Odysseus's honour.
523	But these things Olympian Zeus knows, dwelling in the upper air,
524	whether before the marriage he will bring them an evil day.
As he spoke thus, a bird flew on the right,
a hawk, the swift messenger of Apollo; and in its feet
it held a dove and plucked it, and shed the feathers on the ground
midway between the ship and Telemachus himself.
And Theoclymenus called him apart from his comrades
and clasped his hand, and spoke a word and addressed him:

Telemachus, not without a god did the bird fly on the right;
532	for I knew, seeing it face to face, that it was an omen.
533	There is no other race more kingly than yours
534	in the land of Ithaca, but you are always mighty.
And discreet Telemachus answered him:
He spoke, and addressed Piraeus, his trusty comrade:

Piraeus son of Clytius, you in other things most of all
541	obey me among my comrades who followed me to Pylos;
542	and now take this stranger to your house
543	and treat him kindly and honour him, until I come.
And Piraeus, famed for his spear, answered him:

Telemachus, even if you should stay here a long time,
546	I shall look after him, and he will lack no hospitality.
So saying he went aboard the ship, and bade his comrades
embark themselves and loose the stern cables.
And they quickly went aboard and sat at the oars.
And Telemachus bound fair sandals under his feet,
and took up a valiant spear, tipped with sharp bronze,
from the deck of the ship; and they loosed the stern cables.
They pushed off and sailed to the city, as Telemachus,
the dear son of divine Odysseus, had bidden.
And he, striding quickly forward, was carried by his feet until he reached the farmyard,
where were his swine very countless, among which the swineherd
slept, a good man, kindly in mind to his masters.
